>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
The November midterm elections are now eight days away.
President Trump was in Michigan yesterday campaigning
for Republican Senate nominee
and former Congressman Mike Rogers.
In his remarks, Trump referred
to Rogers' Democratic opponent,
Abdul Al-Sayed, as a jihadist, as a Thai-Smatric bar
with Michigan Public Radio reports,
Al-Sayed's campaign is pushing back on the president.
>> The attack has become something of a closing argument
in Michigan's Senate race.
Republican candidate Mike Rogers recently released an ad
saying Al-Sayed supports terrorists
and is, quote, "funded by people who finance Hamas."
Independent fact checkers have rejected those claims.
During the event, President Trump brought the father
of a man killed during the September 11th terror attacks
on stage.
He repeatedly called Al-Sayed Mohammed
and said Al-Sayed shouldn't be allowed on airplanes.
>> He would be the only senator that will have to go
through a metal detector before he's allowed to go
into the Senate.
I want him to have a metal detector.
>> The Al-Sayed campaign called the remarks "fearmongering."
For NPR News, I'm Itai Smatric bar in Port Huron.
>> In Alaska, Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola
is recovering from injuries sustained in a weekend car crash.
Liz Ruskin with Alaska Public Media has more.
>> Anchorage police say Peltola
and family members were taken to the hospital Saturday
after another vehicle rear-ended theirs.
Her campaign says she has minor injuries
and will be back on the trail Tuesday.
A spokesperson says there's no reason
to believe the collision was politically motivated.
Meanwhile, her attorneys are asking a judge
to quickly dismiss a Justice Department lawsuit.
It seeks to block the state from certifying the election
if Sullivan narrowly loses, pending an investigation
to see if voters were confused
by a second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
The senator is listed on the ballot
as the Republican incumbent.
For NPR News, I'm Liz Ruskin in Anchorage.
>> Brazil's left-wing president has won
that country's election after ranking second
in the initial round of voting.
Catherine Osborne has more from Rio.
>> A downtown Rio Plaza pulsed with surprised relief
after President Luis Anacio Lula da Silva was elected
for a fourth non-consecutive term.
He defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro,
the son of former President Shair Bolsonaro.
The possibility of another Bolsonaro presidency sent Lula
supporters into the streets to campaign by the tens of thousands
in recent weeks.
Their attempt to swing votes paid off.
Lula's victory runs counter
to a right-wing wave sweeping Latin America.
He's promised to continue standing up
to President Trump's aggressive approach toward the region.
For NPR News, I'm Catherine Osborne in Rio de Janeiro.
>> This is "NPR News" from Washington.
Security forces in Jordan say they've made three arrests
in connection with last week's attack
on a Greek Orthodox Church.
Authorities say each of those arrested was wounded
in an exchange of gunfire with security personnel.
The attack on the church south of Amman left nine people dead
and more than a dozen others wounded.
So far, no group has claimed responsibility for that attack.
A startup company in Texas is working to produce a new
generation of military and police dogs
through genetic engineering.
But as NPR's Windsor Johnston reports,
scientists say the technology may be years away
from delivering on that promise.
>> The startup Warhound has raised $200 million
to develop cloned and genetically engineered dogs
with improved health and working abilities.
Cornell University animal geneticist Heather Hewson says
the technology exists, but scientists still don't know
which genes control traits like endurance and behavior.
>> I do appreciate the high-risk, high-reward really reaching
for the stars type of projects, which I think this is doing.
One of my big things of being cautious,
this isn't going to happen overnight.
>> Warhound's website says it's certified
by the American Humane Society, but in a statement to NPR,
the organization says its partnership
with the company is still evolving.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
>> The World Series is shifting from Milwaukee to central Florida
for tonight's game three between the Brewers
and the Tampa Bay Rays.
The Brewers lead the fall classic two games to none.
I'm Dave Mattingly, NPR News in Washington.
